title: A prayer for protection
hook: the Tenth Guru's quiet prayer asking to be sheltered

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten savaiye closed, and your line was love, not display. Now a new bani begins, a quieter one.

Some prayers are made for a crowd, sung by a whole hall at once. Others are made for one person, very quietly: under your breath in the car on the way to the hospital, at three in the morning when the house makes a noise, on a plane as the wheels leave the ground. The Tenth Guru, who wrote war poetry and praise as wide as the sky, also wrote one of those. A small, close prayer, whose own heading calls it a request.
screen: `PRAYERS MADE FOR A CROWD.` → `AND PRAYERS UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `THE TENTH GURU WROTE ONE.`

segments.voice: Benti means a humble request, the kind you make to someone greater than you, standing at their door. Chaupai is the meter: verses whose lines fall into four parts. Its heading in the Dasam Granth reads, roughly, the poet speaks: a request, in chaupai. It's short enough to learn by heart, which many Sikhs do. It's one of the five banis of the Sikh morning, it's in the evening Rehras, and it's recited while the amrit is prepared. One honest note: Sikhs don't all stop it in the same place. Some traditions recite a longer version, some a shorter one, with a few extra verses at the end. Both are said with devotion, and this path follows the common pattern without ranking either. The prayer opens with four lines, and its whole shape is in them. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. Notice what isn't there: no list of demands, no bargaining, no I'll do this if you do that. Just a hand, a heart, feet, and belonging. And notice who is praying: a Guru who led his people through years of war. Sikhs don't hear Chaupai as a frightened prayer. They hear the request of someone who knew that being brave is not the same as being alone.
screen: `BENTI: A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `CHAUPAI: LINES IN FOUR PARTS.` · `MORNING, EVENING, AND AT AMRIT.` · `HAND, HEART, FEET, BELONGING.` · then, large: `SHELTER ME.`

segments.voice: If you can, find Chaupai Sahib in Gurmukhi or transliteration and read the opening four lines aloud, slowly, even if you stumble on the sounds. If not, sit with the four ideas, one breath each: a hand, a heart's wish, resting at the feet, being taken as someone's own. If you pray, say Waheguru after the fourth; if not, notice which of the four you most needed today.
Benti Chaupai. A humble request in four-part verse: the Tenth Guru's short prayer for shelter, said morning and evening and at the amrit ceremony.
Your line: shelter me. Two words, small enough for any moment. Day three hundred seventy.

screen: `DAY 370 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PROTECT ME WITH YOUR HAND.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib every morning as part of the Nitnem and again within the evening Rehras, and many also say it before travel, at night, or in times of fear.

what a scholar hears: the heading 'kabiovach benti chaupai', the poet speaks, a request in chaupai; the poem stands at the close of a long section of the Dasam Granth, and its recited length varies by tradition.

chat.who: a friend on a long flight
chat.says: What kind of prayer is Chaupai? Does it bargain with God for protection?
options: No; it's a humble request: your hand, my heart's wish, your feet, take me as yours.
Yes; it promises daily recitation in return for keeping every danger away.
It's a battle cry, written to be shouted by a whole army before a fight.
